entry: American [[Cable television|cable television]] network and flagship property of The Cartoon Network, Inc. Launched on October 1, 1992, it was the first 24-hour single-genre cable channel with animation as its main theme, and it primarily broadcasts animated series for children. The evening block [[Adult Swim]] targets young adults. The network reached a peak of 100 million households in 2011 and was available in approximately 66 million U.S. pay television households as of November 2023. It was later brought under common ownership with its long-time rival [[Nickelodeon]].

Process of shaping material by scraping away portions of it with [[Tool|tools]]. The technique applies to any material solid enough to hold a form when pieces are removed, yet soft enough to be scraped with available tools. Unlike methods using malleable materials such as [[Clay|clay]], [[Fruit|fruit]] and melted [[Glass|glass]], which are shaped while soft and then harden, carving generally requires much more work. Relief carving cuts a design into a flat surface to make it three-dimensional; chip carving and whittling remove small pieces from a solid block, usually of wood; sculptural carving shapes a lifelike form. Stone and wood carving is a means of making [[Sculpture|sculpture]]. Carved figures date to the Upper Paleolithic era, including the ivory Venus of Hohle Fels, carved around 40,000 years ago in what is now Germany. Durable stone was carved for long-lasting reliefs in [[Ancient Egypt]].

British-American actor, one of classic Hollywood's definitive leading men. Grant grew up in an impoverished family in [[Bristol]], England, and performed in [[Vaudeville|vaudeville]] during the 1920s before moving to Hollywood in the early 1930s. He starred in romantic screwball comedies including *The Awful Truth* (1937), *Bringing Up Baby* (1938), *His Girl Friday* (1940) and *The Philadelphia Story* (1940). He made four films with director [[Alfred Hitchcock]], among them *Suspicion* (1941) and *Notorious* (1946). Grant was nominated twice for the Academy Award for Best Actor, for *Penny Serenade* (1941) and *None but the Lonely Heart* (1944), and received an Academy Honorary Award in 1970. He retired from film acting in 1966 to pursue business interests and was married five times.

Largest city of [[Morocco]] and its economic and business centre (pop., 2024: 3,218,036). Situated on the Atlantic coast, it is the most populous city in the [[Maghreb]] and the ninth-largest in the [[Arab world]], and Greater Casablanca has over 4.27 million inhabitants. Its port is one of the largest artificial ports in [[Africa]] and the third-largest in [[North Africa]]. The Casablanca Stock Exchange is Africa's third-largest by market capitalization as of December 2022, and most major Moroccan companies have their headquarters in the city. After the 1755 earthquake, the ʿAlawi sultan Mohammed ben Abdallah rebuilt it and renamed it ad-Dār al-Bayḍāʾ, "The White House." The city hosted the 1943 Casablanca Conference, where Allied leaders of [[World War II]] planned the campaign against Axis forces in North Africa.

Romantic drama film directed by Michael Curtiz. Starring [[Humphrey Bogart]], [[Ingrid Bergman]] and Paul Henreid, it is set in Vichy-controlled [[Casablanca]] during [[World War II]]. An American expatriate, Rick Blaine, must choose between his love for Ilsa Lund and helping her husband, Czechoslovak resistance leader Victor Laszlo, escape the Nazis. Based on the unproduced play *Everybody Comes to Rick's*, it was shot at Warner Bros. Studios in Burbank, California, from May 25 to August 3, 1942. Released nationally in January 1943, it was a solid rather than spectacular success at first. It won three Academy Awards: Best Picture, Best Director for Curtiz, and Best Adapted Screenplay. In 1989 the [[Library of Congress]] selected it for the inaugural class of the National Film Registry.

American disc jockey, actor and radio presenter of [[Lebanon|Lebanese]] descent. He created and hosted the countdown program *American Top 40*, beginning with the weekend of July 4, 1970, and remained its host until 1988. He was the first actor to voice Shaggy Rogers in the [[Scooby-Doo]] franchise and also voiced Robin in *Super Friends* (1973–1985). He provided many commercial voiceovers and voices for children's programs such as *Sesame Street*.

Tropical evergreen tree (*Anacardium occidentale*) of the family Anacardiaceae, which yields a nut and an accessory fruit called the cashew apple. Native to tropical South America, it was spread by Portuguese explorers in the 16th century to India and other tropical regions; they took it to [[Goa]] between 1560 and 1565. Dwarf cultivars, which mature sooner and yield more, are the most profitable. In 2023, 3.9 million tons of cashew nuts were harvested globally, led by [[Ivory Coast]] and India. The shell and raw seed are toxic, and the shell contains an allergenic resin, anacardic acid, so the nut must be shelled and then roasted or steamed before eating. The apple's juice is made into drinks or distilled into liquor, and shell derivatives are used in varnishes, lubricants and paints.

Fine [[Fiber|fiber]] obtained from cashmere, pashmina and other breeds of [[Goat|goat]]. It has been used to make [[Yarn|yarn]], [[Textile|textiles]] and clothing for hundreds of years. The name derives from an anglicization of [[Kashmir]], associated with the Kashmir shawl that reached Europe in the 19th century. The fiber is collected during the spring [[Moulting|moulting]] season. China and [[Mongolia]] are leading producers as of 2019, with Afghanistan third. Overgrazing to increase production has turned grasslands in Asia into deserts, increasing local temperatures and causing air pollution that has traveled as far as Canada and the United States.

King of Poland (r. 1333–1370) and the last Polish king of the Piast dynasty. His foreign policy prioritized stability over military expansion, normalizing relations with the Kingdom of [[Bohemia]] and the [[Teutonic Order]], often through treaties and arbitration. He accepted the loss of [[Silesia]] to Bohemia but annexed Red Ruthenia, enlarging the kingdom. He codified Polish law in the Statutes of Wiślica and Piotrków, reinforcing royal authority, and earned the unofficial title "the Polish Justinian." His reign also saw towns founded under Magdeburg rights, the building of stone [[Castle|castles]] and protection for Jewish communities. He founded the University of [[Kraków]] in 1364, which remains one of the oldest institutions of higher learning in the world. Having no legitimate male heir, he was succeeded by his nephew [[Louis I of Hungary]], ending the Piast dynasty and creating a personal union with [[Hungary]].

Force on the macroscopic boundaries of a confined space, arising from quantum fluctuations of a [[Field (physics)|field]]. It was named after Dutch physicist Hendrik Casimir, who predicted it for electromagnetic systems in 1948. Two uncharged conductive plates in a [[Vacuum|vacuum]] a few nanometers apart experience an attraction or repulsion, depending on their arrangement; the effect is best described in terms of the [[Zero-point energy|zero-point energy]] of a quantized field. In 1997 Steven K. Lamoreaux measured the force to within 5% of the theoretical value. The effect is significant in aspects of [[Nanotechnology|nanotechnology]] and plays a role in the chiral bag model of the nucleon.

Facility for [[Gambling|gambling]], often built near or combined with [[Hotel|hotels]] and resorts. The term comes from Italian *casa*, "house," and originally denoted a small country villa or social club. The first known European gambling house, the Ridotto, was established in [[Venice]] in 1638 to provide controlled gambling during the carnival season. Gambling was outlawed in the early 20th-century United States, but it was legalized in [[Nevada]] in 1931, leading to the rise of [[Las Vegas]]. Common games include [[Roulette]], [[Baccarat]], [[Blackjack]] and craps. All casino games have a mathematically determined house edge, and [[Slot machine|slot machines]] are among the most popular forms. [[Macau]] is the largest gambling market in the world, having surpassed Las Vegas in revenue.

German Romantic landscape painter. Born in Greifswald on the [[Baltic Sea]] in what was then Swedish Pomerania, he studied in [[Copenhagen]] from 1794 to 1798 before settling in [[Dresden]]. His often symbolic, anti-classical works show contemplative figures silhouetted against night skies, morning mists, barren trees and Gothic ruins, conveying a subjective response to nature. His work brought him early renown, but it fell from favour in his later years, and he died in obscurity. A revival began with an exhibition of 32 of his paintings in Berlin in 1906, and his work influenced Expressionists and later Surrealists. His popularity rose under [[Nazism]], then declined sharply as his paintings were associated with German nationalism. Since the 1970s he has been regarded as one of the most important artists of German Romanticism.

Extinct population of [[Tiger|tiger]] (*Panthera tigris tigris*) native to Central and West Asia. Its range extended from eastern Turkey and northern Iran across the [[Caucasus]] and Central Asia to northern Afghanistan and [[Xinjiang]] in western China. It inhabited sparse forests and riverine corridors until the 1970s and was regarded as a distinct subspecies until it was assessed as extinct in 2003. Genetic studies indicate it was closely related to the [[Siberian tiger]], and the two populations probably formed one continuous population until the early 19th century. The last confirmed individuals were sighted in [[Tajikistan]] in 1971.

Woody [[Shrub|shrub]] of the spurge family, [[Euphorbiaceae]] (*Manihot esculenta*), grown for its starchy tuberous root. Native to South America, it is cultivated throughout the tropics and subtropics, usually as an annual crop. It is the third-largest source of carbohydrates in tropical food, after [[Rice]] and [[Maize]], and more than 500 million people depend on it. Cassava is exceptionally drought-tolerant and can grow on poor soil. Nigeria is the largest producer, and Thailand is the largest exporter of cassava [[Starch|starch]], called tapioca. Sweet and bitter varieties both contain toxins, and improperly prepared roots can contain enough [[Cyanide|cyanide]] to cause poisoning. The common name derives from the 16th-century French or Portuguese *cassave*, from the [[Taíno]] *caçabi*.

Analog [[Magnetic tape|magnetic tape]] format for audio recording, officially named the Compact Cassette. It was invented by Lou Ottens and his team at the Dutch company [[Philips]], and introduced in August 1963; Philips licensed the patented format to other manufacturers from 1966. Developed for dictation, it was widely adopted for music after Dolby B noise reduction became common in the mid-1970s. From 1983 to 1991 it was the most popular format for new [[Music|music]] sales in the [[United States]]. The [[Polyester|polyester]] tape is wound between two miniature spools inside a small plastic shell, and both sides can be played.

Northern [[Constellation|constellation]] and asterism named after the vain queen of Greek mythology. Its distinctive W shape is formed by five bright stars, and it was among the 48 constellations listed by the 2nd-century Greek astronomer [[Ptolemy]]. In myth, Cassiopeia boasted of her beauty, angered [[Poseidon]] and was placed in the sky to circle the north celestial pole. The constellation contains Cassiopeia A, the brightest extrasolar radio source above 1 GHz, which is a [[Supernova|supernova]] remnant. [[Tycho Brahe]]'s supernova of 1572 flared brightly here. Fourteen star systems have been found to have [[Exoplanet|exoplanets]], and a rich section of the Milky Way runs through the constellation.

Genus *Casuarius* of large flightless [[Bird|birds]], native to the tropical forests of New Guinea, the Moluccas and northeastern [[Australia]]. Three species are extant: the southern cassowary, the fourth-tallest and third-heaviest living bird, smaller only than the two ostrich species and the emu; the northern cassowary, the most recently discovered and most threatened; and the dwarf cassowary. Genetic evidence suggests the emu is their closest living relative. Adult southern cassowaries stand 1.5 to 1.8 m tall. Cassowaries are shy, but when provoked they can inflict serious, even fatal, injuries and are often labeled "the world's most dangerous bird," although the [[Common ostrich]] kills two to three humans per year in [[South Africa]].

Class of iron–carbon [[Alloy|alloys]] containing more than 2% carbon and about 1–3% silicon. Its low melting temperature, good fluidity and wear resistance make it suitable for pipes, machine parts and [[Automotive industry|automotive]] parts such as cylinder heads and gearbox cases. Carbon, at 1.8 to 4% by weight, forms [[Graphite|graphite]] flakes in grey cast iron, which deflect cracks, or spherical nodules in ductile cast iron, which stop them. White cast iron holds its carbon as very hard but brittle cementite. Cast iron is brittle except for malleable grades and is notoriously difficult to weld. The earliest artifacts date to the 8th century BC in what is now [[Jiangsu]], [[China]]. In the 15th century it was used for cannons in Burgundy, France, and England. The first cast-iron bridge, the Iron Bridge in Shropshire, England, was built in the 1770s by Abraham Darby III.

Fixed social group into which an individual is born, within a system of [[Social stratification|social stratification]]. Members are expected to marry within the group (endogamy), often follow lifestyles linked to an occupation, and hold a ritual status within a hierarchy. The paradigmatic example is the rigid division of [[India]]'s [[Hinduism|Hindu]] society, whose roots lie in ancient [[South Asia]]. The term is also applied to morphological groupings in eusocial insects such as [[Ant|ants]], [[Bee|bees]] and [[Termite|termites]]. The English word derives from Spanish and Portuguese *casta*, meaning race or lineage; the Portuguese first applied it to Indian social groups, and the spelling is attested in English from 1613. Caste-like systems have also been reported in [[Africa]].

Social classification based on [[Caste|caste]], practised in [[India]] since ancient times. The system was originally centered on four varnas: [[Brahmin|Brahmins]] (priests), Kshatriyas (rulers and warriors), Vaishyas (traders and merchants) and Shudras (labourers). Outside it are the [[Dalit|Dalits]] (also known as "Untouchables") and [[Adivasi|Adivasis]] (tribal peoples). The emergence of jati introduced thousands of castes and subcastes, and the [[British Raj]] furthered the system through census classifications. An estimated 98% of contemporary Indians, including non-Hindus, identify with a caste. After independence in 1947, India banned caste discrimination and adopted affirmative action policies, but caste-based discrimination, segregation and violence persist.

Fortified residence built during the [[Middle Ages]] mainly by [[Nobility|nobility]] or royalty. Scholars usually define a castle as the private fortified residence of a lord, distinct from a palace or villa built mainly for pleasure. European castles originated in the 9th and 10th centuries, after the [[Carolingian Empire]] fragmented among lords and princes who used them to control their surroundings and launch raids. Early castles relied on a central keep; in the late 12th and early 13th centuries, towers and [[Fortification|concentric defence]] emerged, partly from [[Crusades]] technology. Although [[Gunpowder]] reached Europe in the 14th century, castle building was affected only when [[Artillery|artillery]] could break stone walls in the 15th century, and true castles then declined. The word derives from Latin *castellum* and entered English shortly before the [[Norman Conquest]] of 1066.

1997 action role-playing game by Konami for the [[PlayStation (console)|PlayStation]] and [[Sega Saturn]]. A direct sequel to *Castlevania: Rondo of Blood*, it stars Dracula's dhampir son Alucard, who explores Dracula's castle to prevent his father from regaining his power. It reintroduced the exploration and role-playing elements of *Castlevania II: Simon's Quest*. It initially sold poorly, but became a sleeper hit with over 700,000 units sold in the United States and Japan, and is often cited among the best video games of all time. It is considered the definitive pioneer of the Metroidvania genre, combining [[Castlevania]] with [[Metroid]].

Gothic horror action-adventure video game series and media franchise created by Konami. The series is largely set in the castle of [[Count Dracula]], arch-enemy of the Belmont clan of vampire hunters. The first game appeared in 1986 on the Famicom Disk System (known in [[Japan]] as *Akumajō Dracula*), and the early entries were side-scrolling platformers. *[[Castlevania: Symphony of the Night|Symphony of the Night]]* (1997) returned to nonlinear exploration and role-playing elements, and many later entries adopted its gameplay model. Together with [[Metroid|Super Metroid]], it popularized the Metroidvania genre. Spanning four decades, the franchise has appeared on consoles, [[Personal computer|personal computers]] and [[Mobile phone|mobile phones]], and includes comic books and a critically acclaimed animated television series.

Surgical, chemical or other action that disables the [[Testicle|testes]] of a male. Surgical castration is usually bilateral orchiectomy, while chemical castration uses pharmaceutical drugs. Castration greatly reduces the production of sex hormones such as [[Testosterone|testosterone]] and [[Estrogen|estrogen]] and can cause sterilization. It has been used for slavery, such as the [[Eunuch|eunuchs]] of the [[Ottoman Empire]], and as a terror tactic in warfare; it was incorporated into Chinese law during the [[Zhou dynasty]]. In the [[United States]], [[Thomas Jefferson]] proposed a Virginia bill reducing the punishment for rape, polygamy or sodomy from death to castration. Today it is used to treat [[Prostate cancer]]. In animals it is often called neutering.

Person in [[Military|military]] service, combatant or noncombatant, unavailable for duty through [[Death|death]], injury, [[Disease|illness]], capture or [[Desertion|desertion]]. In military usage, a casualty is any person lost to a unit through death, wounds, sickness, capture or desertion; the term is not synonymous with fatality. The number of casualties is the number of unit members not available for duty. The [[NATO]] alliance defines a battle casualty as one incurred as the direct result of hostile action. A civilian casualty is a civilian killed or wounded by military action. In civilian usage, dating from 1844, a casualty is a person killed, wounded or incapacitated by an event such as a violent incident or disaster, and non-fatal injuries count too.
